analysis.one_liner: Taxes offshore profits of companies that renounce U.S. incorporation through corporate inversions.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 52 House sponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in April 2017 and never received a markup or vote; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When a U.S. company moves its legal headquarters to a low-tax country while keeping its business and management in the United States — a practice called a corporate inversion — this bill would treat it as still American for tax purposes. Before any company could expatriate, it would owe tax on the profits it has parked in offshore subsidiaries, and its offshore stock would be taxed as if sold at current value. The goal is to make fleeing U.S. taxes a money-losing move.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and the U.S. Treasury. When corporations shift profits abroad or renounce U.S. incorporation, the federal revenue they stop paying has to be made up by someone — individual taxpayers, or through more borrowing. The bill would keep that money in the U.S. tax base and remove the financial incentive for companies to relocate their paper headquarters overseas.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Individual taxpayers and the U.S. Treasury

how_it_helps.text: Before a company completes a corporate expatriation, the bill requires it to pay tax on the accumulated deferred foreign income of its controlled foreign corporations, ending the practice of leaving offshore profits untaxed until repatriation.

Any stock of a controlled foreign corporation held by an expatriated entity would be treated as sold at fair market value on the expatriation date and taxed, so a company cannot escape U.S. tax on its accumulated gains by moving its legal domicile.

The bill expands the definition of corporate inversion, so foreign corporations that acquire a U.S. company while keeping more than 50% ownership with the former U.S. shareholders, or keeping management and control primarily in the United States, would still be taxed as domestic corporations.
The bill overrides tax treaties for these transactions, closing off arguments that treaty obligations exempt inverted companies from the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-based multinational corporations that have built up untaxed offshore profits and might otherwise move their legal domicile to a low-tax country. They would owe a large one-time tax bill at the moment of expatriation, and companies that complete inversions would remain fully taxable as U.S. corporations if they keep management and control here.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to inversions completed after January 4, 2017 — months before it was introduced in April 2017 — meaning deals already done could be recast and taxed under rules that did not exist when they were completed.

The bill only taxes the deferred offshore income at the moment a company expatriates; a company that stays in the United States keeps deferring tax on offshore profits indefinitely, so the bill penalizes leaving without fixing the underlying deferral system for companies that remain.

Critics of anti-inversion legislation have long argued that U.S. worldwide taxation with deferral puts American-headquartered multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors taxed on a territorial basis, and that stricter rules can push U.S. companies into being acquired by foreign firms rather than merging as the surviving parent — a real cost an honest supporter of the bill would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented problem — companies renouncing U.S. incorporation while keeping their business here — and its main cost falls on the specific companies doing it, not on the general public. The retroactive January 4, 2017 cutoff is the weakest part of the design, since it reaches deals closed before the bill existed. It is also narrower than a full fix of offshore profit deferral, since companies that never leave face no change. On balance, it is a focused anti-avoidance measure whose costs are concentrated on a small group of companies and whose benefit is a broader, fairer tax base.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2017 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to a vote; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on April 5, 2017 with 51 cosponsors, all Democrats, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The committee took no further action; the full action history ends with the referral, so the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

The Ways and Means Committee's chair was a Texas Republican, and the House Republican majority of that Congress set the committee's agenda; no anti-inversion tax bill was brought to a committee vote in the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations that keep untaxed offshore profits and retain the option to move their legal domicile to a low-tax country; they continue deferring U.S. tax and no company that inverted after January 4, 2017 faces the new one-time tax. The Treasury also forgoes the revenue the bill would have raised.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would take away the financial benefit of renouncing U.S. incorporation: companies would owe tax on their accumulated offshore profits the moment they expatriate, and inverted companies keeping management in the U.S. would remain fully taxable as domestic corporations. That directly removes a costly avoidance route whose burden otherwise shifts to other taxpayers.

Firms that plan and execute inversion transactions would lose a product line if the bill eliminated the tax benefit of inversions, while companies that stay would need advice navigating the expanded definitions. The bill's anti-avoidance rules expressly cover intermediaries and step transactions designed to get around it.
